## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why is recognizing the right object insufficient to authorize a robot to reach for it?_

A request to pick a mug names an outcome but leaves the machine to determine where to grasp, how much force to apply, and how long the observation remains useful. A correct label can accompany an uncertain handle position, and a correctly located mug can move while the model computes. Treating either prediction as an unrestricted command lets an error in meaning or timing become a physical collision. The engineer must translate the request into a bounded target, retain the evidence that supports it, and provide a refusal path when that evidence is insufficient. Independent checks limit the target's validity and the effort available to pursue it; trajectory planning must still find a feasible motion, and the permission path must still decide whether that motion may execute. These distinctions keep learned intent on the proposal side of the causal boundary, before a mistaken request becomes motion that software cannot undo.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Ground natural-language directives into metric affordance frames, continuous motion predicates, and verified geometric goal sets
- Emit the Intent Specification contract from parent belief records with explicit error envelopes, task tolerances, and effort ceilings
- Derive a target-evidence horizon from task tolerance and target drift, and distinguish it from the stopping deadline
- Decide when grounding ambiguity or a wrong-object premise requires refusal rather than admission
- Evaluate terminal reachability within one evidence window and select guarded, renewed stages for a longer approach
- Design hardware lease expiry that revokes motion authority even when the issuing process hangs or crashes

:::

## Grounded Affordances {#sec-intent-grounded-affordances}

When the warehouse mobile manipulator is told to "pick the red mug" from the takeaway conveyor, the directive specifies an outcome but leaves path, force, and deadline unresolved. A motor inverter accepts electrical commutations, not language. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2] can propose candidate actions or targets, but their update cadence depends on model parameter counts and edge hardware accelerators, executing at frequencies ($0.5\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$) orders of magnitude slower than local real-time control. If a target moves during neural inference, a stale proposal consumes physical clearance before execution even begins. The system therefore requires dated geometric evidence, bounded capability requests, and an independent permission path that can withdraw authority while the deliberative model is silent.

For the mug, grounding means selecting a physical feature, locating it relative to the robot, and bounding the interaction with it. A pose combines position and orientation; $SE(3)$ denotes the space of these poses, while $SO(3)$ denotes orientations alone. A wrench combines force and torque. The notation below packages those familiar physical quantities so that a candidate grasp can be checked independently of the words that suggested it.

To an engineer trained on digital vision-language models, the directive "pick the mug" might sound like a solved classification task: a cross-attention map highlights the mug, and an autoregressive decoder outputs an action token. In natural language processing, the directive is a discrete sequence of linguistic tokens $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \dots, z_k)$ sampled from a vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$. In transformer latent space, these tokens map to continuous embedding vectors $\mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ where vector distance reflects statistical co-occurrence across text corpora. Yet discrete semantic tokens carry zero physical dimensions (no meters, seconds, or Newtons), zero coordinate frames, zero inertial awareness, and zero physical extent. In embodied physics, grasping an object is not an isolated mathematical point or a categorical label; it is an action-relative physical relation governed by geometric **affordances**\index{Affordances!grasp envelopes} [@gibson1979ecological]. In ecological psychology, an affordance defines what an environment offers, provides, or furnishes to an active agent. In modern robot learning, we demystify this concept from first principles: an affordance model does not produce a vague qualitative abstraction, but evaluates a **spatial probability distribution over valid continuous action parameters**:
$$\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathcal{O}, \mathbf{z})$$
where the continuous action parameter vector $\mathbf{a} = (\mathbf{T}_{\text{grasp}}, \hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}}, w_{\text{aperture}}, \mathbf{w}_{\text{contact}}) \in SE(3) \times \mathbb{S}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathbb{R}^6$ specifies the candidate grasp pose, approach vector, finger aperture, and contact wrench profile, conditioned on dense 3D sensor observations $\mathcal{O}$ (such as RGB-D point clouds or signed distance fields) and natural-language directive $\mathbf{z}$.

Each functional feature on an object establishes an **affordance coordinate frame** $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ rigidly attached to the object's body frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{obj}}$. To bridge the semantic gap between discrete words and physical interaction, this action parameter distribution must be grounded into concrete physical parameters:

1. *Spatial Grasp Center & Pose $\mathbf{T}_{\text{grasp}} = (\mathbf{R}_{\text{grasp}}, \mathbf{p}_{\text{grasp}}) \in SE(3)$:* The 3D translation $\mathbf{p}_{\text{grasp}} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ locates the grasp center in metric base-frame coordinates, while the orientation $\mathbf{R}_{\text{grasp}} \in SO(3)$ aligns the gripper fingers with the workpiece surface tangents.
2. *Directional Approach Vector $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}} \in \mathbb{S}^2$:* A unit vector specifying the proposed direction of approach. The full gripper geometry and surrounding occupancy must still establish whether that approach has a clear corridor.
3. *Jaw Aperture Clearance $w_{\text{aperture}} \in \mathbb{R}^+$:* The finger opening span required to envelop the object geometry prior to contact closure.
4. *Contact Wrench Profile $\mathbf{w}_{\text{contact}} = [\mathbf{f}_{\text{contact}}^\top, \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{contact}}^\top]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^6$:* The contact force and torque profile that governs physical interaction upon contact. Under contact mechanics, grasping requires establishing normal squeeze forces $f_n$ along opposing contact normals such that tangential shear forces $\mathbf{f}_t$ satisfy the Coulomb friction cone condition $\|\mathbf{f}_t\| \le \mu f_n$. The grasp's available wrench envelope must contain the task's required resisting wrenches, including those opposing external gravitational loads $\mathbf{w}_{\text{ext}} = [0, 0, -mg, 0, 0, 0]^\top$ and dynamic inertial accelerations during transit without exceeding the workpiece's structural crush limit $f_{\text{crush}}$. Force closure is a stronger geometric property: the contact arrangement can resist a disturbance in any wrench direction under its idealized force assumptions. Supporting this task still requires adequate capacity under finite force limits.

For the red mug, these parameters specialize across its physical features: the rim affordance frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{rim}}$ requires low gripping force to avoid crushing fragile ceramic or spilling liquid; the cylindrical body frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{body}}$ requires wide parallel finger span and high normal force to prevent slipping; the handle affordance frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{handle}}$ requires a six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) grasp pose that aligns the gripper fingers with the ear of the mug while respecting joint travel and torque limits. Under contact mechanics, opposing contact points must lie within mutually opposing friction cones to resist external gravitational and dynamic disturbance wrenches without slipping, while normal squeeze force $f_n$ remains strictly below structural crush thresholds.

Connecting words to physical targets is the robotics manifestation of the **symbol grounding problem**\index{Symbol grounding problem} [@harnad1990symbol]: a symbol needs a sensorimotor connection to the physical entity it denotes.[^fn-intent-symbol-grounding] For the mug, that connection is the measured handle frame, its calibration chain, and the interaction limits. A plausible label or generated coordinate supplies none of those bounds by itself. A wrong proposal must remain containable even when the model is confident.[^fn-intent-hallucination-containment]

Independent geometric checks test candidate affordances in $SE(3)$ against obstacle clearance, inverse-kinematics feasibility, and contact limits before trajectory optimization. Contact-rich proposals may also undergo simulation checkouts, whose conclusions remain conditional on the modeled geometry, friction, and dynamics. These checks make an affordance useful to a planner by identifying physically plausible interactions; they do not replace admission of the resulting motion.[^fn-intent-affordance-space]

A symbolic action such as `Grasp(Mug, Handle)` expresses the task, but its preconditions need physical tests. Noisy perception does not directly establish that the handle is clear or the gripper aligned. Here, **motion predicates**\index{Motion predicates!definition} connect those task conditions to measured geometry and contact quantities:

1. *Pre-contact approach predicate:* $P_{\text{approach}}(\mathbf{x}) \iff \|\mathbf{p}_{\text{TCP}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{pre}}\| \le r_{\text{tol}} \land \arccos(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\text{TCP}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}}) \le \theta_{\text{tol}}$, requiring the end effector tool center point (TCP, the coordinate origin at the robot's gripper tip—distinct from the network Transmission Control Protocol) frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{TCP}}$ to align with the affordance approach axis $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}}$ within spatial tolerance $r_{\text{tol}}$ and angular tolerance $\theta_{\text{tol}}$.
2. *Guarded contact predicate:* $P_{\text{contact}}(\mathbf{w}) \iff f_{\min} \le \|\mathbf{f}_{\text{contact}}\| \le f_{\max}$, ensuring that contact forces remain sufficient for friction grip while strictly bounded below structural crush limits.
3. *Spatial clearance predicate:* $P_{\text{clear}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathcal{M}) \iff \min_{\mathbf{o} \in \mathcal{M}} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{o}\| \ge d_{\text{margin}}$, checking the point $\mathbf{x}$ against stored obstacle geometry in $\mathcal{M}$ (@sec-memory). This point test alone does not establish clearance for the gripper, links, or their swept volumes; those require the later full-path check.

The position and orientation tolerances define a **geometric goal set** $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} \subset SE(3)$\index{SE(3)!target goal set}:
$$\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} = \left\{ \mathbf{T} = (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{p}) \in SE(3) \;\middle|\; \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{target}}\|_{\mathbf{E}} \le 1, \; \angle(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}_{\text{target}}) \le \theta_{\text{tol}} \right\}$$ {#eq-intent-goal-set-se3}
The contact and clearance predicates remain separate, phase-specific task constraints; they are not encoded by this pose region. Here $\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{target}}\|_{\mathbf{E}} = \sqrt{\sum_{i \in \{x,y,z\}} \left(\frac{p_i - p_{\text{target},i}}{r_i}\right)^2}$ denotes spatial containment within the task tolerance ellipsoid with principal semi-axes $\mathbf{r} = (r_x, r_y, r_z)$, and $\angle(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}_{\text{target}}) = \arccos\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{R}_{\text{target}}) - 1}{2}\right)$ bounds geodesic orientation divergence on $SO(3)$ (equivalent to $2 \arccos(|\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{q}_{\text{target}}|)$ when orientations are represented as unit quaternions). If the terminal grasp pose lies outside $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}}$, the task can fail: position error exceeding $r_i$ causes the gripper fingers to strike the mug rim or close on empty air, while angular tilt beyond $\theta_{\text{tol}}$ jams the fingers against the handle opening, tripping joint torque monitors or shattering the workpiece.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ The running machine's intent horizons, the arm's transit lower bound, the   │
# │ mug intent lapse and its arm stop onset, the latch contact at brake command,│
# │ and the Class 3 plant.                                                      │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_force_rate,
    fmt_heat_capacity,
    fmt_power,
    fmt_temperature,
    fmt_temperature_rate,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    check,
)
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_target_evidence_horizon,
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_contact_force,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus chapter-local scenario inputs ─────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; lease chosen)

delta_t_stall_intent = 200.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (stalled proposer holds the mug target)
delta_t_stall_arm = 200.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (unbraked contact interval)
v_drift_slow = 20.0 * millimeter / second  # category: illustrative (slow-drift case in the figure)
t_intent_tail = 650.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (high-tail intent inference, as in the figure)
d_target_offset = 300.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption: gripper-to-handle distance at proposal)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: evidence horizons, mug intent lapse, latch contact ───────────
# Mug on the conveyor: untracked and tracked target-evidence horizons. Both
# horizons charge the 3 mm initial error against the 15 mm tolerance.
grasp_error_budget = (AISLE.grasp_tolerance - AISLE.grasp_initial_error).to(millimeter)
tau_ev_untracked = calc_target_evidence_horizon(AISLE.grasp_tolerance, AISLE.grasp_initial_error, AISLE.v_conveyor).to(millisecond)
tau_ev_tracked = ((2 * grasp_error_budget / AISLE.a_conveyor_slip) ** 0.5).to(millisecond)
t_intent_period = (1.0 / RM.intent_rate).to(millisecond)
err_at_intent_period = (AISLE.grasp_initial_error + AISLE.v_conveyor * t_intent_period).to(millimeter)
err_excess_at_period = (err_at_intent_period - AISLE.grasp_tolerance).to(millimeter)
t_tail_overrun = (t_intent_tail - tau_ev_untracked).to(millisecond)
tau_ev_slow_drift = calc_target_evidence_horizon(AISLE.grasp_tolerance, AISLE.grasp_initial_error, v_drift_slow).to(millisecond)

# Dynamic reachability: the TCP speed ceiling bounds the reach inside the tracked
# horizon, and a proposal farther away fails the transit lower bound.
d_reach_tracked = (RM.tcp_speed_limit * tau_ev_tracked).to(millimeter)
d_reach_untracked = (RM.tcp_speed_limit * tau_ev_untracked).to(millimeter)
t_transit_floor = (d_target_offset / RM.tcp_speed_limit).to(millisecond)

# Mug intent lapse: a stalled proposer holds the target; untracked drift at the
# conveyor speed, tracked drift from residual slip only; arm stop onset after
# intent expiry is one permission tick, one bus cycle, and the brake onset.
err_stalled_untracked = (AISLE.grasp_initial_error + AISLE.v_conveyor * delta_t_stall_intent).to(millimeter)
err_stalled_tracked = (AISLE.grasp_initial_error + 0.5 * AISLE.a_conveyor_slip * delta_t_stall_intent**2).to(millimeter)
t_arm_onset_after_expiry = (AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)

# Latch contact: force at brake command, then the arm stop that keeps it under the limit.
latch_profile = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(scenario=AISLE)
df_dt = latch_profile["df_dt"]
f_at_brake_onset = latch_profile["f_at_brake_onset"]
x_remaining = latch_profile["x_remaining"]
a_arm_needed = latch_profile["a_arm_needed"]
t_arm_stop = latch_profile["t_arm_stop"]
delta_x_unbounded = (AISLE.v_latch_approach * delta_t_stall_arm).to(millimeter)
f_unbounded = calc_contact_force(AISLE.k_latch, delta_x_unbounded)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ──────────────────────────────
check(abs(tau_ev_untracked.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6, "Untracked mug horizon is 60 ms")
check(abs(tau_ev_tracked.magnitude - 219.09) < 5e-3, "Tracked mug horizon is 219 ms")
check(abs(grasp_error_budget.magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-6, "Mug error budget is 12 mm")
check(abs(err_stalled_untracked.magnitude - 43.0) < 1e-6, "Stalled untracked target sits 43 mm off")
check(abs(err_stalled_tracked.magnitude - 13.0) < 1e-6, "Stalled tracked target sits 13 mm off")
check(abs(t_arm_onset_after_expiry.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-6, "Arm stop onset within 22 ms of intent expiry")
check(abs(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "TCP speed ceiling is 1.0 m/s")
check(abs(t_intent_period.magnitude - 200.0) < 1e-6, "5 Hz intent period is 200 ms")
check(abs(err_at_intent_period.magnitude - 43.0) < 1e-6, "Error at the intent period")
check(abs(tau_ev_slow_drift.magnitude - 600.0) < 1e-6, "Slow-drift horizon in the figure")
check(abs(t_tail_overrun.magnitude - 590.0) < 1e-6, "Tail overrun past the untracked horizon is 590 ms")
check(abs(d_reach_tracked.magnitude - 219.09) < 5e-3, "TCP reach inside the tracked horizon is 219 mm")
check(abs(d_reach_untracked.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6, "TCP reach inside the untracked horizon is 60 mm")
check(abs(t_transit_floor.magnitude - 300.0) < 1e-6, "Transit floor for the offset proposal is 300 ms")
check(t_transit_floor > tau_ev_tracked, "Offset proposal fails the transit lower bound")
check(abs(AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease is 60 ms")
check(abs(f_at_brake_onset.to(newton).magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Force at brake command")
check(abs(x_remaining.magnitude - 0.1525) < 5e-5, "Latch compression left is 0.15 mm")
check(abs(a_arm_needed.magnitude - 2.95) < 5e-3, "Arm stop premise is about 3 m/s^2 (2.95)")
check(abs(t_arm_stop.magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "Arm stop takes about 10 ms")
check(abs(f_unbounded.to(newton).magnitude - 2400.0) < 1.0, "Unbraked contact model")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ──────────────────────────────────────────────
class IntentLeaseArchetypes:
    # Mug on the conveyor
    v_conveyor_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_conveyor, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    r_tol_str = fmt_length(AISLE.grasp_tolerance, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    e0_str = fmt_length(AISLE.grasp_initial_error, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    tau_untracked_str = fmt_latency(tau_ev_untracked, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_tracked_str = fmt_latency(round(tau_ev_tracked.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    a_slip_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_conveyor_slip, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(RM.intent_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_intent_period_str = fmt_latency(t_intent_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_intent_infer_str = fmt_latency(RM.intent_inference_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    err_at_period_str = fmt_length(err_at_intent_period, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    err_excess_str = fmt_length(err_excess_at_period, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    v_drift_slow_str = fmt_velocity(v_drift_slow, unit=millimeter / second, precision=0)
    tau_slow_drift_str = fmt_latency(tau_ev_slow_drift, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_intent_tail_str = fmt_latency(t_intent_tail, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tail_overrun_str = fmt_latency(round(t_tail_overrun.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    # Dynamic reachability on the arm
    d_reach_tracked_str = fmt_length(round(d_reach_tracked.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_reach_untracked_str = fmt_length(d_reach_untracked, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_target_str = fmt_length(d_target_offset, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_transit_floor_str = fmt_latency(t_transit_floor, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    # Mug intent lapse and the admitted mug lease
    err_budget_str = fmt_length(grasp_error_budget, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_stall_intent_str = fmt_latency(delta_t_stall_intent, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    err_stalled_untracked_str = fmt_length(err_stalled_untracked, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    err_stalled_tracked_str = fmt_length(err_stalled_tracked, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_arm_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_arm_onset_after_expiry, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second))
    # Latch contact
    k_latch_str = fmt_sci_qty(AISLE.k_latch, newton / meter, precision=1)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    df_dt_nms_str = fmt_force_rate(df_dt, unit=newton / millisecond, precision=0)
    f_at_brake_onset_n_str = fmt_force(f_at_brake_onset, precision=0)
    f_lim_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_remaining.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_needed.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(round(t_arm_stop.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_stall_arm_str = fmt_latency(delta_t_stall_arm, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    delta_x_unbounded_mm_str = fmt_length(delta_x_unbounded, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    f_unbounded_n_str = fmt_force(f_unbounded, precision=0, commas=True)
    # Permission loop
    f_permission_str = fmt_frequency(RM.permission_rate, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
```

The goal region is a task requirement, not an estimate of where the target lies. The **task tolerance region**\index{Tolerance region!3D spatial}\index{Intent record!spatial tolerance region} specifies how much terminal error the grasp permits; estimator covariance describes uncertainty about the target itself. For the machine's mug grasp, the approved task profile allows `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` of translational error. The proposal must carry a conservative target-error envelope that fits within that tolerance, with the motion check accounting for the remaining tracking error. Enlarging the tolerance to accommodate a poor observation would change the task rather than improve the observation.

Before any candidate affordance is packaged into an intent proposal, the system executes **affordance validation and scoring**\index{Affordances!validation}\index{Affordances!scoring}. When open-vocabulary foundation models predict multiple candidate grasp frames on an object, an affordance scoring function ranks candidate frames across kinematic, geometric, and semantic dimensions:
$$\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}) = w_{\text{sem}} S_{\text{sem}} + w_{\text{manip}} \frac{\mu(\mathbf{q})}{\mu_{\max}} + w_{\text{clear}} \frac{d_{\text{margin}}(\mathcal{M})}{d_{\max}} + w_{\text{align}} (\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\text{TCP}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}})$$ {#eq-intent-affordance-score}
where $S_{\text{sem}} \in [0, 1]$ represents visual-linguistic alignment from cross-attention maps, $\mu(\mathbf{q}) = \sqrt{\det(\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{J}^\top(\mathbf{q}))}$ is Yoshikawa's manipulability index at inverse kinematics configuration $\mathbf{q}$ (favoring configurations with greater local freedom of motion), $d_{\text{margin}}(\mathcal{M})$ evaluates signed Euclidean distance to obstacle geometry in spatial memory $\mathcal{M}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\text{TCP}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}}$ measures directional alignment with the affordance approach vector. The Jacobian maps joint motion to tool motion, so a loss of its rank signals a direction the tool cannot follow locally. A singularity can occur inside the joint range, and a high manipulability score does not establish distance from a joint limit. Joint travel therefore needs a separate check. The intent engine confirms whether candidate frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ is kinematically reachable within workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, whether gripper jaw aperture clears the object width, and whether a collision-free approach cone exists. If validation fails or candidate referents remain unresolved, the system must not execute an ungrounded guess; it triggers an explicit **intent grounding refusal**\index{Intent grounding refusal!definition} (`ERR_GROUNDING_AMBIGUITY`).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The belief record a lease consumes (evidence epoch, initial error, growth law) is specified in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema.
:::

Memory can supply a spatial belief with an expiry (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion); it cannot decide what action that belief authorizes. **Intent**\index{Intent} closes that gap by connecting high-level task semantics to a bounded physical goal. It specifies an admissible, time-bounded target before the trajectory planner of @sec-planning constructs a continuous motion profile to reach it.

[^fn-intent-symbol-grounding]: **Symbol Grounding Problem**\index{Symbol Grounding Problem}: Stevan Harnad's 1990 formulation argues that syntactic manipulation alone does not give symbols intrinsic meaning. In physical AI, grounding binds a proposed label to dated sensor evidence, calibrated metric frames, and task-specific physical checks. Without that binding, a planner may optimize toward the wrong physical target.

[^fn-intent-hallucination-containment]: **Semantic hallucination containment**\index{Safety!hallucination containment}\index{Grounding!semantic containment}: Unlike disembodied text generation where hallucinations degrade conversational coherence, robotic hallucinations command physical momentum. Containment requires packaging high-level outputs into typed proposal contracts with verifiable metric bounds before execution.

[^fn-intent-affordance-space]: **Affordance space parameterization**\index{Affordances!spatial parameterization}: In robot learning, affordances are parameterized as continuous spatial probability fields or reachability manifolds over the Lie group $SE(3)$. Parameterizing reachability as an explicit manifold enables low-level controllers to evaluate physical feasibility before invoking computationally intensive trajectory optimizers.

::: {#dfn-intent-grounding-refusal .callout-definition title="Intent grounding refusal"}

***Intent grounding refusal***\index{Intent grounding refusal!definition}\index{Refusal!grounding ambiguity} is the admission rule whereby an embodied system explicitly rejects semantically ambiguous natural-language directives, returning a typed failure status (`ERR_GROUNDING_AMBIGUITY`) rather than executing ungrounded maximum-likelihood guesses across physical clearance margins.

1.  **Significance**: Rejects a proposal when a task-specific ambiguity test (@sec-intent-failure-modes) fails, before that proposal reaches trajectory generation.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a trajectory planning failure that cannot find a collision-free path to a valid goal, grounding refusal rejects the goal itself as physically ungrounded or ambiguous before the planner is invoked.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Forcing an argmax token decode or nearest-neighbor guess when candidate referents remain unresolved, driving the physical plant toward an arbitrary or hazardous target.

:::

Whatever the model proposes must also remain bounded in time. @Fig-intent-frequency-gap separates the deliberative model, local tracker, permission loop, and drive. Even a model running at $50\text{ Hz}$ can exhibit tail latency ($P_{99} \gg P_{50}$). Faster inference increases proposal throughput but does not establish a worst-case response deadline or verify a target's physical feasibility. A conveyor target whose evidence expires between model updates needs a validated local observation path or a task pause. The figure's rates are illustrative; @sec-intent-goals-expire compares the machine's intent cadence with its conveyor evidence horizon.
