Grounding an open-ended directive therefore produces a dated **intent proposal**. The first design decision is how to turn the selected image region into a metric target without losing its identity, uncertainty, or evidence time. Only then can the independent permission path decide what bounds that target may carry.

## Semantic Request Translation to Geometric Proposals {#sec-intent-request-to-proposal}

A natural language instruction becomes dangerous when an unverified semantic hypothesis commands motion. When an operator or high-level supervisor asks for the red mug, an onboard vision-language foundation model parses the character stream, projects image features into a shared embedding space, and selects a candidate visual bounding region. From those pixels, the network extracts an estimated pose in $SE(3)$ and writes coordinate values into a memory buffer. At the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), an ungrounded string of tokens becomes a requested destination; if admitted, it reaches the causal boundary as mass, velocity, and current.[^fn-math-semantic-metric]

If the visual backbone associates the language token with an adjacent fixture or an unlabeled calibration target, the resulting coordinate vector $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ enters the trajectory pipeline as an authoritative physical goal. Because a low-level motor drive measures only encoder pulses, winding temperatures, and phase currents, it cannot evaluate whether the coordinate it tracks corresponds to the intended mug or to an empty stretch of belt.[^fn-math-vlm-lipschitz] Furthermore, extrinsic transform errors ($\Delta \mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}}$) arising from wrist mounting compliance, mechanical payloads, thermal expansion, or link elasticity propagate directly into metric goal bias. High semantic confidence from a vision backbone masks underlying geometric calibration drift, reinforcing why the proposal must carry conservative base-frame error bounds rather than raw point coordinates. The grounding process must produce an explicit geometric proposal that includes spatial uncertainty, selection evidence, and temporal expiration before any motion planner accepts it.

[^fn-math-semantic-metric]: **Semantic-to-metric transformation**\index{Kinematics!semantic-to-metric}\index{Grounding!metric mapping}: Projecting discrete linguistic embeddings into continuous $SE(3)$ coordinates requires an unbroken coordinate calibration chain from image pixels to actuator base frames. Unmodeled camera mounting compliance or lens distortion maps semantic attention peaks into systematic metric offsets. If the transformation chain lacks rigid extrinsic calibration, high semantic confidence produces large physical tracking errors at the end effector.

[^fn-math-vlm-lipschitz]: **Learned-output sensitivity**\index{Neural network!Lipschitz continuity}\index{Safety!Lipschitz bounds}: A learned pose estimate can change substantially when the image or scene changes, and an empirical confidence score does not bound that change. The permission path limits the admitted target and motion using independently checked geometry, state, and actuator constraints.

### The four-stage open-vocabulary grounding pipeline {#sec-intent-four-stage-pipeline}

The **four-stage open-vocabulary grounding pipeline** separates selecting a referent from locating and acting on it:

1. **Stage 1: Multimodal Perception & Visual Feature Encoding**: High-bandwidth visual streams (RGB-D frames from static cameras or eye-in-hand sensors) are ingested alongside proprioceptive joint states. Executing at batch size one ($B=1$) on edge NPUs or GPUs, a vision backbone (for example, a transformer with $14\times14$ patch tokenization) extracts dense spatial feature embeddings that encode both fine geometry and visual semantics.
2. **Stage 2: 2D Semantic Referent Selection & Open-Vocabulary Prompt Grounding**: Given an unconstrained natural language prompt (e.g., "pick the red ceramic mug"), cross-attention mechanisms align linguistic tokens with visual patch embeddings. Open-vocabulary grounding models such as Grounding DINO [@liu2023grounding] compute attention heatmaps and predict candidate 2D bounding boxes, instance segmentation masks, or normalized spatial location tokens identifying physical referents in image pixel space $(u, v)$. However, a 2D bounding box or pixel mask carries zero metric depth, zero contact surface normal orientation, and zero wrench capability; it identifies where an object appears in the optical projection, not how a physical gripper can contact it.
3. **Stage 3: Metric 3D Lifting & Workspace Unprojection**: Using calibrated camera intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ (focal lengths $f_x, f_y$ and principal point $c_x, c_y$) and synchronized optical depth returns $z = d(u, v)$, the selected 2D pixel coordinates are unprojected into metric camera coordinates: $\mathbf{x}_{\text{cam}} = z \mathbf{K}^{-1} [u, v, 1]^\top = [z(u - c_x)/f_x, \; z(v - c_y)/f_y, \; z]^\top$. Applying the rigid extrinsic transform from the camera frame to the robot base frame, $\mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}} = (\mathbf{R}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}}, \mathbf{p}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}}) \in SE(3)$, transforms the point into base-frame workspace coordinates: $\mathbf{x}_{\text{base}} = \mathbf{R}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}} \mathbf{x}_{\text{cam}} + \mathbf{p}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}}$. The unprojection Jacobian:
$$\mathbf{J}_{\text{lift}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\text{base}}}{\partial [u, v, z]^\top} = \mathbf{R}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{z}{f_x} & 0 & \frac{u - c_x}{f_x} \\ 0 & \frac{z}{f_y} & \frac{v - c_y}{f_y} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
propagates optical measurement noise into Cartesian base-frame covariance: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{base}} = \mathbf{J}_{\text{lift}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{sensor}} \mathbf{J}_{\text{lift}}^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{extrinsic}}$. Because stereo and structured-light triangulation depth standard deviation scales quadratically with distance ($\sigma_z \approx \frac{z^2}{B f} \sigma_{\text{disp}}$ where $B$ is baseline and $f$ is focal length), depth uncertainty dominates lateral uncertainty by nearly an order of magnitude, producing an elongated uncertainty ellipsoid aligned with the optical line of sight. Any unmodeled link compliance or thermal deflection in $\Delta \mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}}$ tilts this elongated uncertainty ellipsoid directly into the robot's physical clearance margin.
4. **Stage 4: Affordance Parameterization & Candidate Goal Generation**: The lifted metric geometry is converted into actionable manipulation hypotheses, formalizing affordance prediction as estimating a spatial probability distribution $\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathcal{O}, \mathbf{z})$ over action parameters $\mathbf{a} \in SE(3) \times \mathbb{S}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathbb{R}^6$. Depending on the architecture, this output may take the form of 6-DoF grasp envelopes with approach cones, continuous 3D attraction/repulsion cost fields [@huang2023voxposer], parameterized motion primitives [@liang2023code], or 256-bin action token distributions [@brohan2023rt1]. Crucially, Stage 4 scores candidate affordance frames $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ using the multi-factor scoring function $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}})$ (@eq-intent-affordance-score), evaluating kinematic manipulability $\mu(\mathbf{q}) = \sqrt{\det(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^\top)}$, distance margins to spatial memory $\mathcal{M}$, and gripper jaw opening clearance. It then parameterizes candidate geometric goal sets $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} \subset SE(3)$ around validated affordance frames and specifies the target motion predicates ($P_{\text{approach}}, P_{\text{contact}}, P_{\text{clear}}$) required for task completion.

Across the physical silicon boundary between the non-real-time Linux Application Processor (AP) and the hard real-time Safety MCU, Stage 4 serializes these hypotheses into a fixed-size, statically verified proposal structure (@tbl-10-intent-proposal-fields).

\Needspace{22\baselineskip}

| Field                  | Representation       | Physical semantics                                                                              | Invariant and admission check                                                         |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `evidence_epoch_ns`    | `uint64_t` (ns)      | Sensor capture timestamp $t_0$ from parent belief record                                        | Must match retained belief epoch; reject if stale or unrecorded                       |
| `affordance_frame_id`  | `uint32_t` (enum)    | Target coordinate frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ (e.g., $\mathcal{F}_{\text{handle}}$) | Must resolve to an approved kinematic frame on the target object                      |
| `predicate_mask`       | `uint32_t` (bitmask) | Requested motion predicates ($P_{\text{approach}}, P_{\text{contact}}, P_{\text{clear}}$)       | Verified against task requirements before planner invocation                          |
| `target_pose_se3`      | `double[7]`          | Proposed pose $[x, y, z, q_x, q_y, q_z, q_w]$ in robot base frame                               | Finite values; unit quaternion ($\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert = 1$); within $\mathcal{W}$ |
| `pos_error_envelope_m` | `double[3]` (m)      | Bounded spatial uncertainty semi-axes $(e_x, e_y, e_z)$                                         | Conservative upper bounds on perception uncertainty; $0 \le e_i \le r_i$              |
| `task_tolerance_m`     | `double[3]` (m)      | Allowable goal region semi-axes $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$                                               | Must meet task profile tolerances; defines $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}}$                |
| `max_linear_vel_mps`   | `double` (m/s)       | Requested tool center point speed ceiling $v_{\max}$                                            | Clamped to plant ceiling; verified against dynamic transit time                       |
| `max_wrench`           | `double[6]` (N, N·m) | Maximum effort ceiling $[F_x, F_y, F_z, \tau_x, \tau_y, \tau_z]$                                | Must not exceed structural yield or sensor saturation limits                          |
| `lease_duration_ms`    | `uint32_t` (ms)      | Requested operational validity horizon $\tau_{\text{lease}}$                                    | Clamped to target-evidence horizon $\tau_{\text{ev}}$ and stopping deadline           |
| `fallback_policy_id`   | `uint32_t` (enum)    | Advisory terminal mode (`HOLD`, `STOP`, `TORQUE_OFF`)                                           | Advisory only; Safety MCU overrides based on load and contact state                   |

: **Untrusted intent proposal fields**: Layout and validation invariants of the candidate proposal transmitted from the Application Processor across the proposal boundary. {#tbl-10-intent-proposal-fields tbl-colwidths="[20,17,33,30]"}

To prevent a learned output from masquerading as a deterministic setpoint, the producer must retain the referent identity and the dated evidence that selected it. Its observation record may contain bounding boxes, attention weights, class probabilities, and a full oriented covariance estimate. The intent proposal (@sec-intent-lease) links to the belief record built from that observation (@sec-memory-spatial-state-schema) by digest and evidence epoch; it carries a candidate pose, conservative base-frame error bounds, task tolerances, and requested expiry, not those full producer-side fields. The independent permission path checks the linked evidence and request against its own limits. An object can shift or become occluded after camera exposure, so a coordinate without a valid evidence link and deadline cannot remain an authorized target.

When a vision-language model sees multiple candidate objects, an argmax can hide an unresolved choice. A digital recommendation can still mislead a user, but it has no direct actuator path; in a robot, an admitted spatial proposal can move mass. If a red glass jar sits beside the red mug on the takeaway conveyor, a poorly grounded guess may select the jar. The system should preserve candidate identity and calibrated uncertainty, refusing a proposal when a task-specific ambiguity threshold is exceeded. The producer can seek a clearer observation or instruction while any previously admitted motion remains subject to its own evidence, lease, and fallback checks.

Formally, **open-vocabulary grounding ambiguity**\index{Grounding!ambiguity} is the condition where multimodal feature projections yield multi-peak posterior distributions, overlapping geometric hypotheses, or unresolvable evidential ties across candidate physical referents, requiring an explicit grounding refusal (`ERR_GROUNDING_AMBIGUITY`) rather than optimistic argmax tie-breaking. A high entropy over the candidate-referent distribution $\mathbf{z}$, $H(\mathbf{z}) > H_{\text{thresh}}$, is one signal of it, and the producer-side filter of @fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease can refuse on that signal before the proposal crosses the proposal boundary. This station adopts a singulated-feed operating rule: independently checked evidence must support a single candidate in the pick window (@sec-intent-failure-modes). That rule avoids unresolved selection at this station; other tasks can admit a uniquely identified target among several objects when their evidence supports the distinction. Low model entropy establishes neither case.

::: {#fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Grounded intent pipeline architecture across the silicon boundary**: Physical AI system architecture partitioning high-capacity deliberative reasoning on the Application Processor (AP) from deterministic safety enforcement on the real-time Safety Microcontroller Unit (MCU). The AP processes multimodal streams (RGB-D vision, natural language prompts, proprioception) through a vision-language backbone and 3D spatial field generator. A producer-side entropy filter ($H(\\mathbf{z}) \\le H_{\\text{thresh}}$) rejects ambiguous bimodal hypotheses before passing a structured intent proposal across the inter-core shared memory boundary (e.g., RPMSG over SRAM). The MCU independently verifies evidence epochs, physical actuator ceilings, and braking stopping reserve before arming a target-validity countdown; trajectory admission remains a separate check (synthesized from Huang et al. [-@huang2023voxposer], Ahn et al. [-@ahn2022saycan], and Gray [-@gray1989leases])." fig-alt="Diagram of vision, prompt, and robot state entering a vision-language backbone and candidate 3D cost field on the Application Processor. A producer-side entropy filter can reject the proposal. A bounded record crosses a silicon boundary via RPMSG/SRAM to a Safety MCU, which checks evidence, physical limits, and stopping feasibility before granting bounded target authority; trajectory permission remains separate."}
![](images/svg/fig10_vla_cross_attention_intent_lease.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease, the selected architecture separates proposal computation from bounded target admission across a silicon boundary. This separation supports independence only when the memory, timing, and fault paths are qualified:

- *Application Processor (AP Domain):* Running a non-real-time operating system (such as Linux) on multi-core host CPUs and neural accelerators, the AP processes computationally intensive visual and linguistic models. Multimodal inputs (RGB-D video, joint telemetry, natural language task instructions) enter a cross-attention vision-language backbone. If candidate referent features indicate high entropy ($H(\mathbf{z}) > H_{\text{thresh}}$), a producer-side filter immediately flags semantic ambiguity. Otherwise, the AP packages the candidate goal, requested wrench limits, and parent belief digest into a static intent proposal message.
- *Inter-Core Transport Boundary:* The proposal crosses from the AP to the real-time core via a deterministic, bounded communication channel, such as a qualified Remote Processor Messaging (RPMSG) implementation over dedicated shared SRAM rings; the protocol name alone supplies no timing bound.
- *Safety Microcontroller Unit (MCU Domain):* Executing a hard real-time operating system (RTOS) or bare-metal control loop, the Safety MCU acts as an independent gatekeeper for untrusted proposals. It treats the incoming proposal purely as an unverified candidate. The MCU validates the evidence epoch against its local monotonic hardware clock, evaluates static workspace and dynamic reachability bounds, checks requested force and velocity limits against configured plant ceilings, and verifies that a collision-free emergency stop profile remains executable within current clearance. Only when all physical invariants are satisfied does the MCU arm a hardware countdown timer ($\tau_{\text{lease}}$) and grant transient tracking authority.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-handle-ellipsoid
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ The mug-handle localization estimate as a 95 percent region, compared with  │
# │ the mug's grasp tolerance axis by axis.                                     │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
import math

# ┌── 1. LOAD: illustrative single-view localization model ────────────────────
sigma_lat_x = 4.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (distant pre-approach wrist-camera view, lateral std. dev.)
sigma_lat_y = 5.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (wrist-camera lateral std. dev.)
sigma_depth = 12.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (wrist-camera depth std. dev.)
chi2_3dof_95 = 7.815  # category: constant (chi-square quantile, 3 degrees of freedom, 0.95)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: principal semi-axes of the 95 percent region ────────────────
k_region = math.sqrt(chi2_3dof_95)
semi_x = (k_region * sigma_lat_x).to(millimeter)
semi_y = (k_region * sigma_lat_y).to(millimeter)
semi_z = (k_region * sigma_depth).to(millimeter)
chi2_cdf = math.erf(math.sqrt(chi2_3dof_95 / 2)) - math.sqrt(2 * chi2_3dof_95 / math.pi) * math.exp(-chi2_3dof_95 / 2)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: the claims the prose makes ────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(chi2_cdf - 0.95) < 1e-4, "7.815 is the 0.95 chi-square quantile for 3 degrees of freedom")
check(semi_x < AISLE.grasp_tolerance and semi_y < AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Lateral semi-axes fit the grasp tolerance")
check(semi_z > AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Depth semi-axis exceeds the grasp tolerance")
check(AISLE.grasp_initial_error < AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Admitted handle estimate fits the tolerance")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ──────────────────────────────────────────────
class HandleEllipsoid:
    sigma_x_str = fmt_length(sigma_lat_x, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_y_str = fmt_length(sigma_lat_y, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_z_str = fmt_length(sigma_depth, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    chi2_str = fmt(chi2_3dof_95, precision=3, commas=False)
    semi_x_str = fmt_length(semi_x, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    semi_y_str = fmt_length(semi_y, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    semi_z_str = fmt_length(semi_z, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

Consider the grounding model's estimate of the red mug's handle from a single wrist-camera view taken at a distance, before the arm begins its approach. In an illustrative calibrated Gaussian localization model, the principal sensor-frame standard deviations are `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_x_str`, `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_y_str`, and `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_z_str`, the largest along the camera's depth axis, which is also the gripper's approach axis. A **95 percent statistical region** around the estimated handle position $\mathbf{p}_0$ uses Mahalanobis squared distance $(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}_0)^T\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}_0)\le\chi^2_{3,0.95}$, where the three-degree-of-freedom quantile is `{python} HandleEllipsoid.chi2_str`, yielding principal semi-axes `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_x_str`, `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_y_str`, and `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_z_str`. @Fig-10-intent-lease-envelope contrasts that uncertain target with the mug's `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance. Both lateral semi-axes fit inside the tolerance, but the depth semi-axis does not, so this estimate fails admission and needs better sensing, a different approach, or refusal.

The worked pick in @sec-intent-lease therefore needs a separately admitted, collision-checked pre-contact approach to acquire better sensing; it cannot use the rejected handle estimate to authorize contact. Its belief record (@sec-memory-spatial-state-schema) comes from a closer wrist-camera capture on the approach, which bounds the initial error at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str`. A statistical region alone leaves a residual tail and cannot certify clearance, so the intent proposal carries conservative base-frame error bounds rather than claiming to encode this covariance.

::: {#fig-10-intent-lease-envelope fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Localization uncertainty and authority expiry**: Panel (a) sketches a statistical target-uncertainty ellipsoid beside the grasp's separate task tolerance. Panel (b) compares counterfactual traces: blue expires and brakes, green continues only with fresh renewals, and red shows motion without a lease. Whether the blue trace rests before the obstacle depends on total pre-brake delay, deceleration, and clearance." fig-alt="Panel (a) shows target-position uncertainty beside the grasp's separate task tolerance region. Panel (b) compares alternative velocity traces: blue authority expires then braking reaches rest if feasible; green dots show fresh renewals in a separate scenario; red continues without a lease toward the obstacle. Physical clearance depends on the complete stopping budget."}
![](images/svg/fig10_intent_lease_envelope.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The renewal traces in @fig-10-intent-lease-envelope are alternative outcomes. Fresh measurements can support continued tracking; a missed renewal invokes the validated stop. Neither outcome repairs the distant view's excessive depth uncertainty, and stopping before the obstacle still depends on the complete response budget.

A detection with a large uncertainty estimate can be rejected by a configured statistical gate. A confident grounding to the wrong physical entity can pass that gate. Suppose instead that a thin-walled glass jar arrives alone where the mug should be, and the vision-language model assigns it a high confidence score when asked for the red mug. The model emits a sharp, low-variance geometric proposal centered on the glass. The trajectory planner receives the coordinate, computes an $SE(3)$ inverse kinematics solution, verifies joint limits, and confirms that the path clears all obstacles in the static environment map. The permission path may find the proposed motion within its configured geometric and force bounds. If those bounds allow the grip force the ceramic mug needs, a smooth, geometrically valid trajectory can crush the glass despite passing the checks.

This failure reveals the boundary between what the permission path can verify and what it must accept as an unvalidated premise. The permission path checks coordinate bounds, kinematic reachability, joint torque limits, and geometric collisions against known occupancy grids. Those physical checks do not establish that the coordinate names the intended object, so the premise that the grasped object is the named object lies outside the permission path's reach. It needs its own task evidence, and it travels with the mug into the handover branch of the release case (@sec-release-case-worked-full) and into the register of claims the machine's evidence leaves open (@sec-frontier-residual-claims-register).

Multimodal feature extraction, cross-attention alignment, and open-vocabulary phrase grounding belong to the computer vision and language literature [@kamath2021mdetr; @gu2022open; @radford2021learning; @liu2023grounding]. A physical AI architecture consumes these grounding models without relying on their internal activations for safety, and even a filtered proposal stream still needs the independent motion-permission check. AutoRT's language-model task filter raised the fraction of acceptable proposed tasks yet still passed a small fraction of unsafe ones, and its deployment relied on joint-force pausing, emergency stops, and human supervision rather than on the prompt (\ref{ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution}) [@ahn2023autort].

::: {#ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution .callout-war-story title="AutoRT task filtering and supervision (2024)"}
**Context**: AutoRT deployed foundation models to propose and filter physical manipulation tasks for fleets of mobile manipulators operating in unstructured human office environments [@ahn2023autort].

**Mechanism**: In an empirical sample of 259 proposed tasks, 228 were initially judged acceptable by human annotators. Applying a secondary large language model (LLM) as a "constitutional" affordance and safety filter improved retention (200 of 214 retained tasks were acceptable), raising the acceptable fraction from 88 to 93 percent. However, the semantic filter still permitted 14 unsuitable or unsafe tasks to pass through to execution.

**Impact**: Relying strictly on high-level prompting or semantic filtering left open a non-negligible tail of hazardous proposals, demonstrating that ungrounded foundation models cannot self-certify physical safety or guarantee collision-free execution in open environments.

**Response**: The system architecture placed physical safety outside the model's domain: deployments supplemented learned proposals with hardware joint-force limits, physical emergency stop buttons, and direct human line-of-sight supervision or physical perimeter barricades.

**Systems lesson**: A learned task filter can improve proposal quality, but it cannot serve as a safety referee. An independent, deterministic permission and fallback path must validate every physical action against real-time plant limits before execution.
:::

Once the mug candidate has a metric frame and a dated record, alternative proposal sources can use the same interface. The sources in @tbl-10-grounding-paradigms differ in what they make available to the planner. SayCan ranks pretrained skills using semantic relevance and learned value [@ahn2022saycan]; Code as Policies generates scripts that call perception and control interfaces [@liang2023code]. VoxPoser supplies spatial value maps (@fig-10-real-grounded-affordance-franka), while OK-Robot selects candidate grasps (@fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding). Each can help turn a request into a useful action candidate, but its output still needs current geometric, effort, and timing checks.

Predicting a plausible coordinate or motion script does not establish physical feasibility. The grounding interface must account for metric geometry, non-penetration, kinematics, and contact mechanics:

1. *Token Discretization and Lack of Metric Topology:* Autoregressive LLMs minimize cross-entropy loss over discrete token vocabularies ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{MLE}} = -\sum \log P(w_t \mid w_{<t})$). Numerical strings like `"0.45"` and `"-0.05"` are represented by vocabulary tokens. Distances in the learned latent space $\mathbb{R}^d$ need not preserve Euclidean metric distance ($\|\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_2\|_2$) in physical 3D space ($\mathbb{R}^3$). Token similarity alone supplies no bound on coordinate error. A consumer therefore needs explicit metric checks rather than treating token likelihood as evidence of geometric continuity.
2. *Absence of Rigid-Body Non-Penetration:* In natural language, words combine freely: the string "the gripper is positioned five centimeters inside the granite table" is syntactically coherent and easily generated by an autoregressive model. In the rigid-body model, solid interiors cannot overlap ($\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{B}_1) \cap \operatorname{int}(\mathcal{B}_2) = \emptyset$), while boundaries may touch at contact. A signed distance field can represent this distinction: $\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = s_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathbf{x}) \min_{\mathbf{y} \in \partial \mathcal{O}} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|$, with $s_{\mathcal{O}}=+1$ outside the obstacle, $-1$ inside, and $0$ on its boundary. A token prediction alone does not establish whether coordinate `[0.45, 0.12, -0.05]` places the robot fingers five centimeters beneath the solid countertop surface. That claim requires independently checked geometry in the stated frame.
3. *Ignorance of Differential Kinematics and Singularities:* A generated coordinate alone supplies neither the manipulator's configuration manifold $\mathcal{C}$ nor its kinematic Jacobian $\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{\partial f_{\text{FK}}(\mathbf{q})}{\partial \mathbf{q}}$. Near kinematic singularities where $\det(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^\top) \to 0$, demanding Cartesian velocity along a vanishing singular direction can require unbounded joint rates in the ideal inverse relation $\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{J}^\dagger \dot{\mathbf{x}}$. Real actuators saturate first; motion along a retained direction need not have this failure.
4. *Neglect of Coulomb Friction and Wrench Equilibrium:* Language descriptions treat "grasping" as an instantaneous symbolic event. Physical manipulation, however, requires adequate task-load wrench capacity: contact forces must reside within Coulomb friction cones $\|\mathbf{f}_t\| \le \mu f_n$ to resist external gravitational and inertial disturbance wrenches $\mathbf{w}_{\text{ext}}$ without slipping, while normal squeeze force $f_n$ remains strictly below structural yield limits. A proposed grasp therefore needs contact geometry and material limits before its wrench request can be assessed.

Geometric verification and simulation provide complementary checks on these proposed interactions:

1. *Deterministic Geometric Verifiers:* Before a foundation model proposal reaches the trajectory optimizer, independent libraries evaluate signed distance fields over the relevant robot geometry to check clearance from non-contact obstacles ($\min_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{B}_{\text{robot}}} \Phi(\mathbf{x}) \ge d_{\text{margin}}$). Inverse kinematics may use closed-form solutions where the mechanism permits them or numerical solvers otherwise. Each returned configuration still needs joint-limit and singularity checks; a determinant threshold ($\det(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^\top) > \epsilon$) is a selected conditioning screen, not a universal distance from singularity. Grasp-quality metrics, such as the Ferrari-Canny metric, can assess the contact wrench envelope under their stated friction and force assumptions. Force closure ($\mathbf{0} \in \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup \mathcal{FC}_i))$) alone does not establish finite capacity for the task loads. These candidate checks precede the full trajectory and contact-phase checks.
2. *Physical Simulation Checkouts:* For contact-rich, dynamic, or non-prehensile tasks (such as sliding, unlatching, or dual-arm handovers), candidate proposals can be checked in accelerated multi-body physics simulation environments (e.g., Isaac Sim or MuJoCo) executing in parallel on edge accelerators. Simulation checkouts integrate forward rigid-body dynamics $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau} + \mathbf{J}_c^\top \mathbf{f}_c$ under frictional contact constraints to evaluate whether the proposed contact sequence causes tipping, jamming, or slippage under realistic contact friction before physical hardware commits kinetic energy.

@Tbl-10-grounding-paradigms summarizes what each paradigm emits and what the downstream physical permission path must independently verify.

::: {#fig-10-real-grounded-affordance-franka fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Manipulator 3D affordance grounding via synthesized value maps**: VoxPoser composes language-guided 3D value maps for robotic manipulation tasks [@huang2023voxposer]. An LLM generates code that establishes 3D attraction fields (green) pulling the end effector toward the target and repulsion fields (red) pushing away from obstacles. The resulting spatial cost fields guide trajectory optimization; however, an independent permission path, torque check, and stopping wrapper remain mandatory before motor actuation. (Source: Huang et al., 2023 [@huang2023voxposer], CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="VoxPoser research figure showing a manipulator and sequential language-guided 3D spatial value maps for several tabletop tasks. The image illustrates proposed objectives and motion planning, not a certified force limit, collision bound, or intent lease. Source: Huang et al., 2023."}
![](images/jpg/fig10_real_grounded_affordance_franka.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

In @fig-10-real-grounded-affordance-franka, Huang et al. [-@huang2023voxposer] turn instructions such as "open the top drawer" into spatial objectives. Attraction toward a handle and repulsion from observed obstacles guide the optimizer toward a useful interaction. The planner must still check the resulting path and actuator demands; an obstacle missing from the observations also remains missing from the generated field.

::: {#fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Open-vocabulary grasp grounding pipeline**: OK-Robot combines candidate grasp generation with language-conditioned object selection and geometric filtering [@liu2024okrobot]. An open-vocabulary detector isolates the target object mask, candidate grasps are sampled across the 3D point cloud, and geometric heuristics prune inadmissible approaches. The resulting grasp pose represents a candidate proposal; bounding tolerances, evidence deadlines, and independent permission checks are an architectural wrapper developed in this chapter. (Source: Liu et al., 2024 [@liu2024okrobot], CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="OK-Robot figure showing a robot camera view, candidate grasps, a language-conditioned target mask, filtering, and a selected grasp pose. The image illustrates proposal generation; it does not show a certified collision check or an expiring intent lease."}
![](images/jpg/fig10_real_open_vocab_grounding.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

In @fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding, Liu et al. [-@liu2024okrobot] separate language-conditioned object selection from geometric grasp generation. A scene-wide grasp sampler supplies candidates, and the selected object mask filters them to the requested referent. The selected pose still requires dated evidence, effort bounds, and expiry before it can support execution.

| Proposal source           | Representation sent downstream                          | Early check                                                | Remaining evidence needed                                                                        |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2D box or mask            | Image region plus measured depth and camera calibration | Reject absent depth or a target outside a validated region | 3D pose error, occlusion, object identity, and swept-path clearance                              |
| 3D feature or value field | Candidate target or cost field in a stated frame        | Reject out-of-workspace targets and stale map cells        | Conservative occupancy, unknown-space policy, actuator and timing bounds                         |
| Action-token VLA          | Decoded action in its trained action range              | Reject out-of-range or inadmissible proposals              | State-dependent physical limit and independent permission; token bins provide no clearance proof |
| Language-selected skill   | Skill identifier with estimated success                 | Rank or decline low-confidence candidates                  | Current preconditions, path feasibility, and separate physical enforcement                       |

: **Grounding representations and admission questions**: Outputs from different model families require different conversions before a physical permission check. {#tbl-10-grounding-paradigms tbl-colwidths="[18,24,24,34]"}
Discretized outputs carry no metric bound, and the two common kinds lack it for different reasons.[^fn-vla-action-discretization] In action-token models such as RT-1 [@brohan2023rt1] and OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla], a decoded token is an empirical index within a normalized training distribution that encodes zero metric clearance to physical obstacles. In vision-language models such as PaliGemma, location tokens quantize normalized image coordinates, which become a metric base-frame pose only through measured depth, a sensor calibration chain, and an uncertainty model whose extrinsic and depth terms can easily dominate the quantization grid itself.

[^fn-vla-action-discretization]: **Action and Location Token Discretization**\index{Vision-language-action!token discretization}: Vision-language-action architectures discretize continuous joint or Cartesian deltas into uniform bins (typically 256 per dimension) over an empirical training range, discarding continuous metric clearance. Similarly, multimodal backbones with location tokens map normalized image coordinates into discrete spatial bins (for example, 1,024 bins in PaliGemma), requiring external camera intrinsics and optical depth unprojection to recover metric coordinates in the robot's physical workspace.

The distant view fails on depth uncertainty, and the wrong-object example fails on a different premise: precise geometry does not establish identity. A useful candidate therefore carries both dated metric evidence and task-specific selection evidence. The handoff must preserve those distinctions while limiting the time and effort available to pursue the target.

## The Intent Handoff and Bounded Authority {#sec-intent-handoff}

When the arm reaches for the red mug, the Brain sends neither joint trajectories nor winding voltages across the proposal boundary. It requests a target region, an expiry, and limits on physical effort. The independent permission path checks those bounds using retained evidence and configured plant limits. Admitting the target allows a planner to seek a motion toward it; it does not admit that motion or give the model access to actuator registers.

The independent permission path evaluates the requested target bounds before the planner relies on them. Host-side geometry work supplies bounded local evidence under a qualified interface; the full scene map does not become MCU-resident merely because a check consumes it. The checks span four mandatory invariants:

1. *Spatial containment invariant:* The proposed geometric goal set $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} \subset SE(3)$ must lie strictly within the robot's reachable workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, and the bounded spatial uncertainty envelope $(e_x, e_y, e_z)$ must fit inside the task tolerance $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$ without intersecting persistent obstacle geometry in spatial memory $\mathcal{M}$.
2. *Temporal freshness invariant:* The sensor evidence epoch $t_0$ must match a retained parent belief record, and the unobserved elapsed time on the Safety MCU's monotonic hardware clock must not exceed the target-evidence horizon $\tau_{\text{ev}} \le (r_{\text{tol}} - e_0) / v_{\text{drift}}$.
3. *Dynamic effort invariant:* Requested tool-center-point velocity $v_{\max}$, acceleration $a_{\max}$, and contact wrench $\mathbf{w}_{\max} = [F_{\max}, \tau_{\max}]^\top$ must remain strictly within actuator thermal ratings, link inertia limits, and workpiece structural yield thresholds.
4. *Certified deterministic fallback invariant:* The robot must possess an independently verified, pre-computed stopping or hold trajectory that brings all moving links to rest within current physical obstacle clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$) if authority is abruptly revoked.

Each invariant addresses a different failure: an uncertain target can exceed the grasp tolerance, old evidence can describe a displaced mug, excessive effort can damage the workpiece, and loss of authority can leave moving mass without a feasible fallback. The Intent Specification (Contract 9), realized as an admitted Intent Lease, records the target bounds that survive these checks. It constrains the trajectory planner (@sec-planning), which must still construct a motion whose path, timing, and stopping behavior the permission path can admit. @Sec-intent-lease collects the resulting fields after their physical meaning has been established.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_p.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Plan node."}
*The Plan node: generating bounded intent leases that constrain autonomous action within verifiable safety limits.*
:::

The candidate's evidence epoch and finite requested expiry\index{Intent record!temporal lease} make temporal validity enforceable without an asynchronous cancellation message from the proposer.[^fn-anti-async-abort] The independent controller checks the admitted deadline and selects a validated hold or stop if the supporting evidence or authority lapses.[^fn-std-iso-watchdog] The deadline mechanism and its drift-derived duration are developed in @sec-intent-goals-expire; here the remaining handoff obligation is to bound the physical effort before that deadline.

[^fn-std-iso-watchdog]: **Hardware watchdog safety monitors**\index{Hardware!watchdog timer}\index{Safety standards!ISO 13849}: A safety design can use an independently clocked watchdog to detect missed renewals and initiate a validated response without the host. Safe Torque Off removes drive torque; it does not by itself hold a suspended load or stop moving mass within a specified clearance.

[^fn-anti-async-abort]: **Asynchronous Safety Event Dispatch**\index{Antipatterns!asynchronous safety cancellation}: Relying on asynchronous cancellation messages or network event dispatch to abort motion introduces non-deterministic queue serialization delays, and every millisecond of that delay is unbraked travel at the base's drive limit. A local countdown can revoke tracking authority on missed renewal.

A target bounded in space and time remains dangerous if the controller is granted unlimited physical effort. The intent proposal therefore requests explicit effort ceilings\index{Intent record!force limits} on tool-center-point velocity, acceleration, and contact wrench. If a vision backbone localizes a surface with small stereo disparity error, placing a goal coordinate two millimeters inside a rigid workpiece, a stiff proportional-integral-derivative (PID) position controller will saturate motor currents attempting to eliminate the persistent error. The integrator winds up, driving inverter phase currents to thermal and overcurrent trip limits while transmitting destructive shock loads into gear teeth. For the arm's guarded approach to the spring-latched cage door, the proposal requests the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire as its contact-force ceiling, well below the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` structural latch limit, and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` approach speed as its velocity cap. The permission path compares each request against independently configured actuator torque-speed limits and task ceilings, admitting only a safe, feasible subset.

The low-level **impedance controller**\index{Impedance controller}[^fn-ctrl-impedance-intent] can reduce contact loads by regulating the relation between motion and force:
$$\mathbf{M}_d (\ddot{\mathbf{x}} - \ddot{\mathbf{x}}_d) + \mathbf{D}_d (\dot{\mathbf{x}} - \dot{\mathbf{x}}_d) + \mathbf{K}_d (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_d) = \mathbf{f}_{\text{ext}}$$ {#eq-intent-impedance-law}
where $\mathbf{M}_d, \mathbf{D}_d, \mathbf{K}_d$ in @eq-intent-impedance-law represent the target virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness matrices, and $\mathbf{f}_{\text{ext}}$ is the environmental force on the robot in the stated Cartesian frame. The reaction force the robot applies to the environment has the opposite sign. Under the controller's validated quasi-static contact assumptions, virtual stiffness relates position error to steady-state contact force:
$$\mathbf{f}_{\text{ext}} \approx \mathbf{K}_d (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_d)$$
Tailoring $\mathbf{K}_d$ along the approach axis can limit this steady-state load. The relation alone does not bound initial impact or peak force: approach speed, passive compliance, sensing delay, and available actuator response must support the contact limit as well.

[^fn-ctrl-impedance-intent]: **Mechanical impedance regulation**\index{Control systems!impedance control}: Impedance control regulates the relation between contact force and motion through effective mass, damping, and stiffness. It can reduce loads within a validated contact regime; the first impact and peak force still depend on approach speed, passive compliance, sensing, and actuator response.

Omitting any of these three bounds leaves a physical machine exposed during communication dropouts or perception stalls. Kinetic stopping distance grows linearly with the delay before braking onset and quadratically with physical velocity (@eq-body-stopping-distance). On a mobile base, whose stopping budget is a spatial clearance, a stalled proposer lengthens the delay term by the entire duration its last proposal retains execution authority. That duration is the chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences, and it directly inflates the unbraked latency term $\tau_{\text{delay}}$. Under the selected stopping model, the checked obstacle boundary must lie beyond this cumulative stopping distance, including sensor delay and uncertainty margins. The selected powered response also requires drive energy, sensing, and actuator authority to survive the fault; logic hold-up alone cannot supply braking torque.

The intent lease bounds how long the high-level target remains justified. Expiration withdraws permission to keep tracking that target and invokes a validated response. It does not replace the chunk lease or remove sensing, communication, actuator, and braking delays from the stopping budget.

::: {#nbk-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure-tradeoff-across .callout-notebook title="Lapsed authority and physical response"}

The two quantitative models below evaluate the physical consequences of stalled computation across distinct manipulation regimes. A stopping calculation requires the total delay to brake onset and the deceleration available from the *current* measured physical state:

1. **The mug intent lapse:** The manipulator reaches for the red mug under an intent proposal admitted without local tracking. At conveyor speed `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_str`, the conveyor consumes the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_budget_str` error budget between the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` initial localization error and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance in `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`. Consequently, the target's sensor evidence expires at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`, as formalized in the mug-handle belief record of @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema. Suppose the application processor stalls during neural inference. A target held for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` by the frozen proposer would sit `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_untracked_str` away from the physical mug, guaranteeing that the gripper fingers close on empty air or strike the rim. The intent lease does not wait for a host recovery packet: at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`, the lease expires, tracking authority terminates, and the arm initiates a controlled stop with onset within `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` (spanning one permission loop tick, one fieldbus cycle, and actuator brake onset). The independently enforced chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences bounds active motion separately; its detection path must remain available under the declared host fault. By contrast, with conveyor velocity compensated and the declared residual-slip bound, a prediction carried for the same `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` inference stall leaves the target only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_tracked_str` off, inside the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` tolerance, because the tracked evidence horizon derived in @sec-intent-goals-expire extends to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. A qualified local tracker can supply new evidence before this horizon; the bound does not claim that a continuously renewed estimate ages for the entire stall. Local tracking is what renders a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` deliberative intent refresh rate viable.
2. **The arm at the cage door:** In mechanical contact with stiff physical environments, contact force does not rise gradually; for contact stiffness $k$, force escalates at the rate $\frac{df}{dt} = k \cdot v_{\text{approach}}$. At the guarded approach speed of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` against the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.k_latch_str` strike plate of the cage door, modeled contact force rises at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.df_dt_nms_str`. A `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire threshold combined with a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_contact_str` contact-loop response yields `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_at_brake_onset_n_str` **at the exact instant the brake command begins**; force continues to rise rapidly while actuator inertia decelerates. Staying strictly below the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` latch yield limit leaves only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.x_remaining_str` of allowable mechanical compression, requiring the arm to decelerate at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.a_arm_str` and come to rest within `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_stop_str`. Whether the manipulator can sustain that peak deceleration depends on actuator torque limits and link inertia. If unbraked motion continues for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_arm_str` due to a delayed abort command, the gripper advances `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.delta_x_unbounded_mm_str` past initial contact, generating `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_unbounded_n_str` in the linear-spring contact model—vastly exceeding structural yield limits and destroying the mechanism.
:::

The mug and latch expose different limits on the same **privilege separation boundary**\index{Privilege separation!intent boundary}.[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent] The proposer requests a target and effort bounds; the independent supervisor must retain a feasible response when target evidence expires or contact changes. This separates deliberation from real-time supervision, extending the behavioral priority separation of early reactive systems [@brooks1986robust].

[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent]: **Privilege separation in behavioral layers**\index{Architecture!subsumption}\index{Control!subsumption}: Rodney Brooks's subsumption architecture established priority-arbitrated behavioral layers on sensory feedback. In physical AI systems, this architecture manifests as an unprivileged deliberative layer proposing targets to a privileged real-time supervisor that validates invariants and enforces safe fallbacks.

The handoff now separates target tolerance, evidence uncertainty, effort, and fallback. The conveyor determines how long those bounds remain useful: even a correctly selected and localized handle moves after capture. Its evidence-growth law supplies the deadline the independent controller must enforce.

## Expiring Goals and Temporal Validity Leases {#sec-intent-goals-expire}

The mug can leave its grasp tolerance while the proposal still names exactly the same coordinate. Target validity therefore needs a deadline derived from physical drift, independent of when the model next produces an output. A temporal lease makes that deadline enforceable even when the proposer stops communicating.

To see why goal expiration must be autonomous and time-bounded, suppose the application processor hangs while the arm reaches for the red mug. The fault that makes cancellation necessary is the same fault that stops the cancellation from being sent, because an explicit abort requires a working sender, scheduler, and communication path. An intent lease must therefore expire on its own. This is principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission} applied to a goal. In distributed systems, Gray and Cheriton [-@gray1989leases] introduced leases to ensure cache consistency without distributed commit protocols: a coordinator grants time-bounded authority that lapses automatically unless renewed, eliminating blocking when a client crashes. In distributed software, an expired lease simply delays a read or write; data in RAM remains static. In physical AI, however, moving links possess kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$). An unexpired lease does not maintain a static cache; it permits moving mass to consume physical clearance. The authority relationship is therefore inverted: the privileged Safety MCU acts as the real-time resource coordinator, granting a transient tracking lease to the unprivileged deliberative layer. If the host operating system stalls, deadlocks in a garbage-collection pause, or crashes under a kernel panic, the Safety MCU does not negotiate or wait for an abort packet: its local hardware countdown timer lapses, atomically revoking tracking authority and engaging an independent, pre-certified fallback profile.[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Kinetic momentum budgets and stopping distance constraints originate in @sec-body-kinetic-momentum.
:::

The lease uses the Safety MCU's monotonic hardware clock. Wall-clock adjustments can change apparent age, and host software callbacks can stall with the process they are meant to supervise. A $50\text{ Hz}$ inference rate does not eliminate $P_{99}$ stalls. An independently clocked countdown instead triggers local withdrawal of tracking authority on expiry. This removes host scheduling from expiry detection; it does not remove communication, actuator response, or deceleration from the physical stopping budget.

The target-evidence deadline follows the rate at which the physical target can diverge from its last measurement. Suppose validated bounds cap relative target drift at $v_{\text{drift}}$ (representing the maximum relative velocity divergence between the robot end-effector frame and the physical target, incorporating both workpiece conveyor motion and unmodeled robot base odometry drift) and initial position error at $e_0$ within the belief record's declared validity region, and the task allows a target error of $r_{\text{tol}}$. Over elapsed time $\Delta t$, unobserved physical divergence expands linearly: $\|\mathbf{x}^*(t) - \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_0)\| \le e_0 + v_{\text{drift}} \Delta t$. Setting this maximum error equal to the task tolerance boundary $r_{\text{tol}}$ yields the linear **target-evidence horizon**:
$$\tau_{\text{ev}} \le \frac{r_{\text{tol}} - e_0}{v_{\text{drift}}}$$ {#eq-intent-lease-drift-bound}

[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]: **Hardware watchdog down-counters**\index{Hardware!watchdog timer}: Detecting a missed renewal is only the first term of the response budget. Drive command propagation, brake engagement, and physical deceleration each add a separately measured term.

When $r_{\text{tol}}\le e_0$, the target is inadmissible at capture: sensor uncertainty alone exceeds the task clearance, and the controller immediately refuses dependent motion. Even when @eq-intent-lease-drift-bound gives a positive horizon, a separate motion-permission check must verify current clearance against total sensing, permission, communication, and brake-onset delay plus physical braking distance, as in @sec-nervous.

When target tracking cancels relative drift velocity ($v_{\text{drift}} \to 0$) but workpiece motion exhibits bounded residual slip acceleration $a_{\text{slip}}$, the tracker predicts the target at time $t$ from evidence captured at $t_0$, denoted $\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t\mid t_0)$. The residual prediction error expands quadratically: $\|\mathbf{x}^*(t) - \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t\mid t_0)\| \le e_0 + \frac{1}{2} a_{\text{slip}} \Delta t^2$. Equating this to $r_{\text{tol}}$ yields the **accelerated evidence horizon**:
$$\tau_{\text{ev,tracked}} \le \sqrt{\frac{2(r_{\text{tol}} - e_0)}{a_{\text{slip}}}}$$ {#eq-intent-lease-slip-bound}
When residual slip acceleration dominates, the accelerated evidence horizon follows @eq-intent-lease-slip-bound. If both linear drift and disturbance acceleration $a_{\text{dist}}$ are simultaneously present, unobserved divergence follows the quadratic root of @eq-mem-occlusion-expansion, shortening the admissible validity window accordingly.

For the red mug on the takeaway conveyor, the grounded target moves at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_str`. A `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance and `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` initial error leave a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` **target-evidence horizon** by @eq-intent-lease-drift-bound. Stretching the horizon to the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` refresh period of the machine's `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` intent model would let modeled target error reach `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_at_period_str`, or `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_excess_str` beyond the tolerance. The intent model, whose inference alone takes `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str`, cannot by itself refresh a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` target for continuous motion. Without a qualified tracker the conveyor must slow or pause, or the task must be refused. At `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_drift_slow_str` drift the same bound gives a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_slow_drift_str` evidence horizon (@fig-10-lease-dynamics-tradeoff).

A qualified local tracker changes the arithmetic. It re-measures the mug on every frame and follows the conveyor's velocity, so the conveyor speed no longer drives the error. The same `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` initial error is still charged against the tolerance, which leaves `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_budget_str` for the residual slip of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.a_slip_str` to consume. Against that budget, residual slip alone sets the tracked evidence horizon that @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline solves, `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. The tracker renews that evidence at its own rate, so the tracker's period plus latency is what must fit inside the horizon. The intent model only re-confirms which mug is meant, and each renewal it sends carries the tracker's fresh evidence rather than the frame the model last read. Whichever horizon applies caps the intent lease on this target (@sec-intent-lease).

::: {#fig-10-lease-dynamics-tradeoff fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Target-evidence horizon and early filters**: Panel (a) plots the bound $\tau_{\text{ev}}\le(r_{\text{tol}}-e_0)/v_{\text{drift}}$; its green region means only that the target remains within the task tolerance. An illustrative 650 ms high-tail inference cannot renew the 60 ms conveyor case. Panel (b) shows early rejection stages that precede the full path and stopping checks." fig-alt="Panel (a): target-evidence validity vs. drift speed, with 600 milliseconds at 20 millimeters per second and 60 milliseconds at 200 millimeters per second for a 15-millimeter tolerance and 3-millimeter initial error. Green means target evidence remains within this model's tolerance, not that motion is safe. Panel (b): sequence and evidence check, workspace prefilter, dynamic lower-bound check, and ambiguity gate leading to the planner. Full path and stopping clearance remain separate checks."}
![](images/svg/fig10_lease_dynamics_tradeoff.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Coupling target-evidence validity to the reasoning model's cadence creates a drift hazard. Suppose a design ties the mug's evidence to the intent model's output rather than to a tracker, so the untracked `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` horizon applies, and a single inference runs to a high-tail latency of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_tail_str`. Extending the target record to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_tail_str` solely to hide that delay would leave its estimate outside the declared error envelope for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_tail_overrun_str`. The `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` limit is an evidence-validity deadline, and only new evidence, checked again against the motion, can extend it; faster compute cannot.

Continuous tracking requires *fresh physical evidence*, not merely a new packet from the same stale frame. A renewal based on a new capture must arrive before the current evidence and admitted authority expire, with capture, processing, transfer, clock uncertainty, and permission time included in its budget. The simple condition $T_{\text{period}}+t_{\text{latency}}<\tau_{\text{ev}}$ is only a necessary scheduling check. When a fresh proposal arrives, the planner may compute a jerk-limited splice\index{Trajectory Generation!jerk-limited splice} from the measured state. It admits that splice only if the swept path, new evidence, and stopping reserve remain feasible; an abrupt target change can instead require refusal or a checked stop.

When the countdown the MCU armed at admission runs out, whether or not the host is still running, the independent controller withdraws the proposal's authority and selects a previously validated response\index{Safety!deterministic terminal state} for the measured load and contact mode. An active position hold needs torque and can protect a suspended payload; controlled deceleration needs brake capability and clearance; torque disable can be suitable for some drives but can release a load or leave momentum uncontrolled. The proposer may request a mode, but it cannot choose the terminal action for the MCU. Admission fails when no response remains feasible from the current state.

Executing an expiring lease safely assumes that the commanded geometric proposal is actually achievable by the physical body. If a proposed coordinate lies beyond kinematic reach\index{Kinematics!workspace reachability} or demands joint velocities that exceed actuator limits\index{Actuator!velocity limits} during the lease window, granting the lease wastes control authority and can trip the drive's overcurrent protection as a motor draws excessive current toward an impossible speed. Determining whether a goal is kinematically and dynamically admissible belongs before the trajectory generator accepts the lease, establishing a physical filter between high-level intent and motion execution.

## Admissible Goal Sets {#sec-intent-admissible-goal-sets}

If the red mug rides past on the far side of the belt, beyond the arm's physical reach from where the base is parked, no sequence of joint torques can bring the gripper to its handle. In an embodied ML system, this physical impossibility must be intercepted at the proposal boundary\index{Proposal boundary!goal filtering}, before the target enters the trajectory optimization queue. When an upstream vision-language model\index{Vision-language model} or diffusion policy emits a candidate Cartesian coordinate, treating that proposal as an unverified candidate protects the real-time motion pipeline from executing—or even attempting to solve—impossible trajectories.

A reachability screen also protects the planner's compute budget. The trajectory optimization problem below previews the work developed in @sec-planning: choose joint motion over time, penalize abrupt changes, and satisfy the target and joint limits. Here the engineering decision is simpler. If a target cannot be reached at all, or a requested terminal move cannot finish before its supporting evidence expires, that request should fail before detailed planning. A longer task can instead request guarded progress under renewable evidence; that is a different request from completing the grasp on one capture:
$$\min_{\mathbf{q}(t)} \int_0^T \left( \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(t)^\top \mathbf{W}_a \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(t) + \dddot{\mathbf{q}}(t)^\top \mathbf{W}_j \dddot{\mathbf{q}}(t) \right) dt \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{q}(0) = \mathbf{q}_0, \; f_{\text{FK}}(\mathbf{q}(T)) \in \mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}}, \; \mathbf{q}_{\min} \le \mathbf{q}(t) \le \mathbf{q}_{\max}$$ {#eq-intent-nlp-trajectory-formulation}
In the non-linear trajectory optimization formulation of @eq-intent-nlp-trajectory-formulation, continuous collision avoidance constraints $d(\mathbf{q}(t), \mathcal{O}) \ge d_{\text{margin}}$ are enforced against spatial memory $\mathcal{M}$. The planning budget depends on the solver, scene, and hardware; it must be measured for the selected implementation. If an out-of-reach target is passed directly to the solver, the forward kinematics constraint $f_{\text{FK}}(\mathbf{q}(T)) \in \mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}}$ has an empty feasibility set ($f_{\text{FK}}^{-1}(\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}}) = \emptyset$). Rather than failing instantly, the non-linear solver consumes its entire computational iteration budget searching gradient space before terminating on an iteration timeout, converting a geometric hallucination from an upstream foundation model directly into real-time compute starvation on the planning core.

To avoid spending the planning budget on an already impossible request, the admission layer first applies two lower-cost checks. Their execution and evidence-query budgets still require qualification:

1. **Static Workspace Manifold Check ($\mathbf{T}_{\text{target}} \in \mathcal{W}$):** Geometric workspace analysis defines the closed spatial manifold $\mathcal{W} \subset SE(3)$ of reachable end-effector configurations given link dimensions, joint travel limits, and mounting geometry [@craig2005introduction; @lynch2017modern].[^fn-math-workspace-manifold] An analytical reachability check evaluates whether the target $SE(3)$\index{SE(3)} pose $\mathbf{T}_{\text{target}}$ resides inside this workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, while an occupancy lookup in spatial memory confirms that the target volume does not intersect persistent static obstacles.
2. **Dynamic Reachability Transit Check:** For a terminal move supported by one evidence record, even if a target lies inside the static workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, it may be physically unreachable within the finite window during which its sensor evidence remains valid. **Dynamic reachability**\index{Dynamic reachability} is the condition that the end effector can transition from its measured state $(\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{v}_0)$ to the target pose within the remaining window $t_{\text{exp}} - t_{\text{now}}$ while respecting its velocity, acceleration, jerk, and thermal torque limits.

Whatever continuous trajectory profile the actuators follow, no physical move covers distance $d = \|\mathbf{p}_{\text{target}} - \mathbf{p}_0\|$ faster than its maximum speed ceiling allows. Here both $\mathbf{p}$ terms are translation vectors in the same Cartesian frame, not full $SE(3)$ poses; orientation feasibility requires a separate check. For terminal completion before the current expiry, a necessary condition is:
$$\frac{d}{v_{\max}} \le t_{\text{exp}} - t_{\text{now}}.$$ {#eq-intent-dynamic-reachability-bound}
Actuator acceleration limits, jerk ceilings, and motor torque-speed curves only lengthen the required transit time. A proposal that violates this inequality cannot promise terminal completion in that window. A request for an intermediate guarded segment may remain feasible if its executed motion and fallback fit the current authority and its continuation requires newly admitted evidence. @Sec-appendix-control-reachability derives triangular and trapezoidal transit bounds and explains how jerk limits change the complete-move check.

The scalar lower bound is an early rejection test, not a path solver. It avoids optimizing a terminal request that is already too late, while leaving acceleration, obstacles, and stopping reserve to the fuller motion check. No rejection fraction or execution-time bound follows from the inequality alone.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Admissible goal regions specify the boundary conditions for spline generation in @sec-planning-continuous-trajectories.
:::

[^fn-math-workspace-manifold]: **Kinematic workspace boundaries and singularities**\index{Kinematics!workspace boundaries}: The kinematic workspace defines the continuous manifold of task-space poses attainable by the manipulator given link geometry and joint travel limits. At a singular configuration the kinematic Jacobian $\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})$ loses rank. A nonzero Cartesian velocity in a lost direction is unattainable at that configuration; approaching the singularity can require unbounded joint rates for that demand in the ideal inverse model. Retained directions can remain usable. Workspace filtering rejects unreachable targets but does not eliminate internal singularities, which require configuration and path checks.

On the arm, the mug's evidence under the qualified tracker stays valid for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str` after its capture. At the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_tcp_str` tool center point (TCP) speed limit, the gripper could cover at most `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_reach_tracked_str` even if the entire window remained. A terminal proposal issued with the gripper `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_target_str` from the handle needs at least `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_transit_floor_str` of transit. It therefore receives `ERR_DYNAMIC_TIME_INSUFFICIENT` if it promises completion on that record. Without the tracker, the full window is only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` and the corresponding speed-only reach is `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_reach_untracked_str`. Processing and transport consume part of either window; acceleration further reduces the reachable distance.
